hints: Start by picturing the plasmid as a closed circle - what must first happen to its DNA backbone before a new gene can be fitted in?
Once the insulin gene with matching sticky ends sits in the opened plasmid, think about which enzyme seals the sugar-phosphate backbone to make one continuous circle again.
Think about how you get the insulin gene in the first place from a cell - if you only have single-stranded DNA made from mRNA, what is needed to make it double-stranded?
For that first step of making DNA from mRNA, recall which viral enzyme reads RNA as a template to build a complementary DNA strand.
walkthrough:
Cutting Open the Plasmid - Restriction Endonuclease**
Think of the plasmid as a closed loop that must be opened. Restriction endonuclease cuts the plasmid DNA and also cuts the donor DNA containing the desired gene, leaving complementary sticky ends ready for joining.

Sealing the New Loop - DNA Ligase**
Once the gene fragment base-pairs with the cut plasmid by its sticky ends, the backbone still has breaks. DNA ligase joins the gene DNA to the plasmid DNA by forming phosphodiester bonds, creating recombinant DNA.

Making Double-Stranded DNA - DNA Polymerase**
Many insulin genes are first obtained as single-stranded cDNA. DNA polymerase builds the complementary DNA strand using base pairing, so you have stable double-stranded DNA that can be inserted.

From mRNA to DNA - Reverse Transcriptase**
To get an intron-free eukaryotic gene, you start from mature mRNA. Reverse transcriptase uses mRNA as a template to synthesise complementary single-stranded DNA (cDNA), which DNA polymerase then makes double-stranded.

Final answer: restriction endonuclease cuts DNA / plasmid; DNA ligase joins DNA with the plasmid; DNA polymerase forms dsDNA / makes a complementary DNA strand; reverse transcriptase uses mRNA as template to make cDNA / complementary ssDNA.

hints: Remember that simply having the coding sequence inside a cell does not mean the cell will use it - what process must start first for protein to be made?
Think about what must physically attach to DNA just before the start of a gene to begin that process.
Consider why a bacterial cell might not recognise a human control sequence, so why a suitable promoter must travel with the gene.
walkthrough:
No Promoter Means No Reading**
A coding sequence alone is silent. For mRNA to be made, the transcription machinery must know where to start. The promoter is that signal region upstream of the gene.

Docking Site for Transcription Machinery**
Transcription factors bind to the promoter, which then allows RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription. Without this, the bacterial RNA polymerase would not recognise and transcribe the inserted human gene.

Switching On and Controlling Expression**
So the transferred promoter ensures the gene is expressed and lets us control or increase transcription. For example, an inducible promoter responds to a specific environmental change, or a strong promoter gives high-level transcription in all tissues.

Final answer: Promoter provides binding site for transcription factors and for RNA polymerase, so the desired gene is transcribed / expressed / switched on; allows control / increase of transcription, e.g. inducible or tissue-specific expression.

hints: Look closely at Fig. 4.1 - compare the small black arrow for direction of transcription in the promoter with the white arrow inside the black insulin gene for each plasmid.
Remember transcription only proceeds in one direction away from the promoter - what happens if the gene points back toward the promoter?
Check plasmid Z carefully - is the thick black gene present at all, or has the cut plasmid simply joined back together?
walkthrough:
Reading Direction Matters**
The promoter arrow shows transcription moves clockwise. The insulin gene arrow shows which strand will be read. For functional mRNA, both arrows must point the same way.

Plasmid X vs Plasmid Y**
In plasmid X the black gene arrow points anticlockwise, opposite to the promoter - it is inserted backwards, so no correct insulin mRNA and no insulin polypeptide. In plasmid Y the gene arrow points clockwise, same direction as the promoter - it is the correct orientation, so transcription proceeds through the gene and insulin is produced.

Plasmid Z Has No Gene**
Plasmid Z shows only the rejoined sticky ends with no thick black insert. The plasmid has closed up without the insulin gene, so it is non-recombinant and cannot produce insulin, though the marker gene is still present.

Final answer: plasmid X - no insulin, gene inserted backwards / wrong way around so not correctly transcribed; plasmid Y - produces insulin, gene inserted correct way around with transcription in same direction as promoter; plasmid Z - no insulin, gene not inserted / plasmid closed up / non-recombinant.
